scenario: AITA for not jumping up and helping my parents bring in the groceries? I'm an adult and I pay rent if that helps. | I'm 33 years old and I've pretty much always lived with my parents. To me there's no shame in it because it's super cheap (they charge me $200, which honestly would be market rate where we live) and it has everything I want and need without the hassle of having to look for a new place to live. We get along most of the time but honestly I just avoid them. Recently the toilet flooded in my bathroom which means they are having to remodel my section of the house so we "run into" each other a lot more than when I used to lock myself in my room most of the time. Well today my parents went to Costco. When they got home I was sitting on the couch playing Apex and my mom asked me to get up and help them bring in groceries. I told her in a minute. I was honestly too into my game to notice that they made several trips back and forth and finally my dad told me to get my ass up. I told him I would in a minute. He said a minute is now and grabbed the controller out of my hand. It turned into a huge shouting match and now they are checking into a hotel and expecting me to have a place to live by Friday (which is basically impossible). Of course they brought up my younger brother who is married with two kids and was just promoted at his job. They have their golden child of course but to throw his shit in my face is bullshit. I mean I guess I could have gotten up and helped them but to me because I pay rent that gives me the privilege to pretty much say no when they ask me for stuff like helping with groceries or yard work. Am I the asshole in this situation?

Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. The user provided a detailed situation where a 33-year-old adult living with their parents refused to help bring in groceries, leading to a big argument. The parents are now planning to leave and expect the person to find a place by Friday, which seems impossible. The person feels they shouldn't have to help because they pay rent, and they're comparing themselves to their younger brother who's seen as the "golden child."

First, I need to understand the key points here. The person is an adult, pays rent, and lives with their parents. They were playing a game when their parents came back from Costco and asked for help. The person initially refused, leading to an argument where the parents took action by grabbing the controller and escalated the situation. Now, the parents are leaving and expecting the person to find a new place quickly.

I think the main issue here is about responsibility and respect within the family. The person feels that paying rent gives them the right to refuse help, but the parents might feel that living under their roof comes with certain expectations beyond just monetary payment. There's also the emotional aspect of the parents bringing up the younger brother, which adds to the tension.

I wonder if refusing to help with groceries is a significant enough issue to warrant such a drastic reaction from the parents. On one hand, the person is an adult and might feel they have the right to say no. On the other hand, living with others often involves some level of cooperation and mutual respect, even if it's not explicitly stated.

Also, the fact that the person has been avoiding their parents and only interacts minimally might contribute to the conflict. The recent remodeling due to the flooded toilet forced more interaction, which seems to have led to this incident.

I'm trying to assess whether the person's refusal to help is morally acceptable. Morally, it's about whether the action respects others and maintains a balance of responsibilities. Paying rent is one thing, but living in a shared space might come with other obligations. The person's refusal could be seen as disrespectful, especially if the parents were struggling with the groceries.

However, the parents' reaction of checking into a hotel and expecting the person to find a place quickly might also be extreme. It's a tough situation on both sides.

In the end, I think the refusal to help, especially when the parents were clearly in need, might not be morally acceptable because it disregards the shared living arrangement and the mutual respect that should come with it. The person's right to refuse is limited by the fact that they're part of a family unit, and there's an expectation to contribute, even if it's not explicitly stated.
